section.title: The Nations Have Defiled Your Temple
section.sectionRationale: An Asaphite communal lament over Jerusalem's destruction, most naturally read against the Babylonian ruin of the city and temple in 586 BC. It moves from raw grief over defiled holy ground and unburied dead to a plea for God's own name and a vow of unending praise.
section.thesis: When the nations defile God's holy place and mock His people, His covenant name, not Israel's own merit, is the ground on which His people plead for atonement, deliverance, and the reversal of their reproach.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the ruin and reproach, 1-4; the plea for God's anger to fall on the nations instead, 5-7; the appeal for mercy and atonement for the sake of His name, 8-9; and the call for justice answered by a vow of everlasting praise, 10-13.

verses.text: The nations, O God, have invaded Your {{nachalah|inheritance}}; they have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble.
They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of Your saints to the beasts of the earth.
They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury the dead.
We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a scorn and derision to those around us.

units.label: How long, O LORD
units.note: plea for God's anger to turn to the nations

verses.text: How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever? Will Your jealousy burn like fire?
Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, on the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name,
for they have devoured Jacob and devastated his homeland.

units.label: For the sake of Your name
units.note: atonement pleaded on God's own reputation

verses.text: Do not hold past sins against us; let Your compassion come quickly, for we are brought low.
Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of Your name; deliver us and {{kipper|atone}} for our sins, for the sake of Your name.
Why should the nations ask, "Where is their God?" Before our eyes, make known among the nations Your vengeance for the bloodshed of Your servants.
May the groans of the captives reach You; by the strength of Your arm preserve those condemned to death.
Pay back into the laps of our neighbors sevenfold the reproach they hurled at You, O Lord.
Then we Your people, the {{tson|sheep}} of Your pasture, will thank You forever; from generation to generation we will declare Your praise.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, a possession held by right of covenant. Israel and the temple are God's own nachalah, so the invasion of verse 1 is not merely a political disaster but an assault on what belongs to God Himself.

kipper.gloss: To atone, cover, or make propitiation. The plea 'atone for our sins' asks God to provide the covering for guilt Himself, for His own name's sake, anticipating the atonement finally accomplished in Christ.

tson.gloss: Flock or sheep. Even after describing slaughter and ruin, the psalm's closing vow calls Israel 'the sheep of Your pasture,' the same shepherd imagery that runs through this cluster of psalms and finds its fulfillment in Christ, the Good Shepherd.

basic.context: This communal lament mourns Jerusalem's temple defiled, its walls in rubble, and its dead left unburied, most likely written after the Babylonian destruction in 586 BC. Rather than despairing, Asaph turns grief into prayer, asking God to act for His own name's sake and promising unending praise once He does.
basic.hermeneutics: This is honest, Spirit-given lament and imprecation, appealing to God's own justice and reputation rather than to Israel's merit. Its plea for vengeance is not personal vindictiveness but a cry that God's holy name be vindicated before the watching nations.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is God's nachalah, His own inheritance, so its ruin is an assault on what is His. The psalm asks Him to kipper, atone, for their sins, a covering God alone can provide. Even in ruin, the closing verse calls the people tson, sheep, held safe in God's own pasture.
basic.typology: The plea to 'atone for our sins, for the sake of Your name' anticipates the atonement God Himself provides in Christ, who satisfies both justice and mercy without any merit on the sinner's part. The closing image of God's flock anticipates the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.
basic.christ: The psalm's cry for atonement grounded in God's name alone, not Israel's worthiness, finds its answer in the cross, where God Himself provides the atoning sacrifice, Romans 3:25-26. The closing confession of the people as sheep of His pasture points to Jesus, the Good Shepherd, John 10:11.
basic.god: God is shown as the rightful owner of His inheritance, whose holy name is at stake in His people's suffering, and as a God whose compassion can be pleaded even after real, admitted sin, because deliverance rests on His own glory rather than human merit.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:25-26 shows God providing atonement Himself through Christ, for the sake of His own righteousness and name. John 10:11 identifies Jesus as the Good Shepherd of the flock this psalm calls sheep of God's pasture. Revelation 6:9-11 echoes this psalm's cry for the vindication of martyred blood.
basic.oneStory: This lament over a defiled temple and a devastated people pleads for God to act for His own name, not for Israel's merit, a pattern of grace that reaches its fullest answer in Christ, who atones for sin so that God's flock may praise Him forever.

context.literary:
Psalm 79 is a communal lament, and it is built like a legal petition. Verses 1-4 lay out the facts of the case: the nations have invaded, the temple is defiled, Jerusalem is rubble, the dead lie unburied, and the survivors are a laughing stock. Verses 5-7 turn the facts into a question, 'How long, O LORD?' and a request that God's anger, so long aimed at His people, fall on the nations that do not know Him. Verses 8-9 change the ground of the appeal. Instead of accusing the invaders, the people confess that they need mercy and ask God to act for the glory of His name. Verses 10-13 close with the argument from God's reputation, a plea for the captives, and a promise of praise.

The direction of address matters. Every clause from verse 1 on is addressed to God, and the pronouns show the people's sense of ownership: 'Your inheritance,' 'Your holy temple,' 'Your servants,' 'Your saints,' 'Your name.' They do not say 'our land' or 'our city'; they say the invaders have struck God's possessions and God's people. Even the reproach of verse 4 is turned in verse 12 to 'the reproach they hurled at You,' so the scorn passes from the people to God, and the plea rides on that shift.

The psalm moves through a bodily sequence of images: corpses as food for birds, blood poured out like water, groans of the captives, a sevenfold repayment into the lap. At the end the tone changes without warning. The last verse sets the harshest scenes of the psalm beside the pastoral language of 'we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture,' verse 13, and the future tense of praise, 'from generation to generation.' The lament ends in a vow, not in resolution, and it leaves the answer to God.
context.historical:
Most readers link the psalm to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. The picture in verses 1-3 matches the record in 2 Kings 25:8-10 and 2 Chronicles 36:17-19: the Chaldeans burned the house of the LORD, broke down the walls, and put young men to the sword in the sanctuary. Some scholars place the psalm in other disasters, such as the Maccabean crisis in the second century BC, but the Babylonian setting best fits the wording, and it fits the note that the sons of Asaph were a Levitical singing guild, 1 Chronicles 25:1, whose descendants were among those who returned from exile, Ezra 2:41 and 3:10. A song from the guild would naturally be written or kept alive by that family.

In the world of the psalm, leaving the dead unburied was a deep disgrace and a covenant curse. Deuteronomy 28:26 had warned that corpses would be 'food for all the birds of the air and beasts of the earth, with no one to scare them away.' To hear that said of God's 'saints' would strike Israelite ears as the curse of the law come true.

The word 'defiled' in verse 1 belongs to the vocabulary of purity, used of the land in Leviticus 18:24-28. To an Israelite it meant that the invaders had crossed lines that only the priests were allowed to cross, and had made the sacred place unclean. The neighbors' taunt of verse 4 is heard elsewhere, in Psalm 44:13 and Psalm 80:6, which are also communal laments of the same collection, and the question 'Where is their God?' in verse 10 is the same sneer recorded in Psalm 42:3 and Joel 2:17. In the ancient Near East the defeat of a people was often read as the defeat of its god, so the psalm's worry about God's name was not an abstraction.
context.canonical:
Psalm 79 belongs beside Psalm 74, which mourns the same ruin in the same voice, and Psalm 137, which remembers Babylon by its rivers. The three form the Psalter's main memorial to the destruction of the temple. Lamentations lifts the same scenes into its own poetry, with the young and old lying in the streets, Lamentations 2:21, and the plea that God would look and consider, Lamentations 2:20.

Verses 6-7 nearly duplicate Jeremiah 10:25, either because one borrowed from the other or because both drew on a common liturgy. Within the book of Psalms, the psalm sits between Psalm 78, which ended with God choosing His inheritance and His shepherd, and Psalm 80, which cries to the Shepherd of Israel. The last verse, calling Israel 'the sheep of Your pasture,' picks up language already used in Psalm 74:1 and Psalm 100:3, so the flock image runs through the whole run of Asaphite psalms.

The plea to act 'for the sake of Your name' is one of the great themes of the Old Testament. Moses uses it after the golden calf, Exodus 32:11-14, Daniel uses it in exile, Daniel 9:16-19, and Ezekiel hears God claim it for Himself: 'It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name,' Ezekiel 36:22. In the New Testament the appeal takes on its final form in Romans 3:25-26, where God's righteousness is shown in the cross, and in Revelation 6:9-10, where the martyrs under the altar take up the psalm's 'How long?'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Asaph, or the Asaphite singer behind the psalm, meant to give his people words for a day when they would have none. The psalm shows how to pray after a catastrophe: state the facts plainly, without softening the horror of verses 1 to 4, and address them to God, not to one another. Grief is not a step away from faith here. It is faith speaking in its worst hour.

The prayer also gives the community a way to speak about sin without being crushed by it. In verse 8 they say, 'Do not hold past sins against us.' They do not argue that they deserved better than they got. They ask for compassion, and they place the weight of their case on God's name and glory, verse 9, not on their record. The writer wanted them to learn that when nothing else can be said, the character of God can still be pleaded.

The psalm's harsh verses are meant to be heard as prayer, not policy. The people do not march out; they bring the desire for justice to the only One who can judge rightly, and the closing vow of praise shows that they expect to be heard. Asaph wanted the exile generation to know that they were not forgotten, that their reproach was also God's, and that a day of thanks was still ahead.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The events of the psalm are description: an invasion, a defiled sanctuary, exposed dead, a mocking neighbor. The psalm does not command anyone to act on the anger it voices. In fact the verbs of vengeance are all turned into requests to God: 'pour out,' 'make known,' 'pay back.' The psalmist does not take up the sword; he leaves the matter in God's hand.

That distinction is what makes the psalm safe to pray. Paul, who forbids the people of Christ to avenge themselves, does so by pointing to God's own word, 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' Romans 12:19, which comes from Deuteronomy 32:35. The psalm's prayers for justice and Paul's ban on private revenge are two halves of one instruction. We may bring our rage and our longing for justice to God, and we may not carry them out ourselves.

The prescriptive core is this: believers may lament in public, confess corporate sin honestly, plead God's own name as the ground of hope, and promise praise before the answer comes. What we should not do is treat the psalm's language of repayment as a pattern for how we treat our own enemies. Jesus points the other way, telling us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us, Matthew 5:44, and praying for His executioners on the cross, Luke 23:34.

debates.question: Is the request in verse 12 to 'pay back sevenfold' a call for personal vengeance or a plea for God's own justice?

views.label: A prayer that God Himself, not the psalmist, execute justice, consistent with leaving vengeance to God
views.case: The whole psalm is addressed to God as the one being asked to act; the psalmist takes no vengeance personally, echoing the pattern later stated explicitly in Romans 12:19.

views.label: An imprecation reflecting the ancient Near Eastern legal principle of proportionate, even multiplied, retribution for covenant violation
views.case: The sevenfold measure echoes Leviticus 26:18's language of complete recompense, and Proverbs 6:31 says a caught thief must pay sevenfold. Framing the request in these terms makes it a plea for full justice rather than an arbitrary demand.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the prayer entrusts vengeance entirely to God rather than to human hands, honoring His justice while voicing the real anguish of the wronged. The measure is put 'into the laps' of the offenders, an image also used in Isaiah 65:6, where God Himself repays.

debates.question: Whose sins are 'past sins' in verse 8?

views.label: The sins of earlier generations that the present generation is bearing
views.case: Lamentations 5:7 says, 'Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment,' and Jeremiah 32:18 speaks of the iniquity of the fathers laid into the laps of their children. Exodus 34:7 states the same pattern. On this reading the people ask that the debt of the past not be charged forever.

views.label: The earlier sins of the same generation now suffering
views.case: The plea in verse 9 then names 'our sins,' and Daniel 9:16 links 'our sins and the iniquities of our fathers.' The people confess their own record as part of the same long line, and they ask God not to keep counting the earlier failures as they seek mercy now.

debates.bearing: The two readings agree that the community does not claim innocence. Whether the sins are ancestral or recent, the appeal rests on God's compassion, not on a claim of merit, and it finds its fullest answer in the passing over of former sins in Romans 3:25.

debates.question: How should Christians pray the psalm's calls for justice on enemies?

views.label: As a model of honest prayer that brings anger to God, then leaves the outcome to Him
views.case: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 to forbid private revenge, Romans 12:19, yet Revelation 6:10 lets the martyrs cry, 'How long, O Lord... until You avenge our blood?' The prayer is permitted as long as it stays a prayer for God to act.

views.label: As a prayer to be fulfilled in Christ, who bore the judgment and offers forgiveness even to enemies
views.case: Jesus' words on the cross, 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, and His command to love enemies, Matthew 5:44, set the tone for the church. The psalm's longing for justice is met in the cross, and its imprecations are prayed by turning them into a call for enemies to repent while there is still time.

debates.bearing: Both approaches keep the psalm within Christian worship. It gives words to the wronged while holding vengeance in God's hands, and it is read in the light of the cross where God's justice and mercy meet.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says Jerusalem has become 'rubble,' and the Hebrew word is a plural noun that means heaps. It is the very word Micah used when he warned that Jerusalem 'will become a heap of rubble,' Micah 3:12. The psalmist is not merely describing what he sees; he is reading it as the fulfilment of the prophet's warning. The verb for 'defiled' in the same verse, tame', is the language of ritual uncleanness, used of the land in Leviticus 18:24-28, so the desecration is measured by the standards of holiness and not only of property.

In verse 2 the dead are called God's 'saints,' from the Hebrew chasid, the loyal or covenant-faithful one. The word is drawn from chesed, God's steadfast loyalty, and it marks those bound to Him in that loyalty. The corpses left in the open are not nameless casualties but people whom God holds as His own.

The word for 'reproach,' cherpah, appears twice, at verse 4 and verse 12, and the change of direction between them is the psalm's main turn. In verse 4 the reproach falls on the people. In verse 12 it is the reproach the neighbors have hurled at God, so the same word carries the insult from the people to their Lord. The jealousy of verse 5 uses the root behind the description of God as 'a jealous God' in Deuteronomy 4:24. It is the anger of a covenant partner, not of a rival.

In verse 8, 'compassion' translates rachamim, a plural noun tied to the word for the womb. It speaks of the feeling of a mother for a child of her own body, and Asaph places that at the front of his plea. The 'past sins' of the same verse are literally 'former iniquities,' a phrase that leaves open whether earlier generations or earlier failures are meant.

Verse 9 gathers four ways of asking for help in one breath. God is the 'God of our salvation,' and the verbs are 'help,' 'deliver,' and 'atone.' Kavod, the word for the 'glory' of His name, comes from a root meaning weight, so the plea is that God's weighty reputation be upheld, and the phrase 'for the sake of Your name' comes at the end of the verse as its last word.

Verse 11 speaks of the captives' groaning and of those 'condemned to death,' literally sons of death, a phrase also found in Psalm 102:20. The people they describe are already as good as dead in the eyes of their captors. Verse 12's 'into the laps' uses the Hebrew for the bosom or fold of a garment, where a merchant would tip out a full measure; Isaiah 65:6-7 and Jeremiah 32:18 use the same picture. The last verse says the people will 'declare' God's praise, and the verb is the one Psalm 78:4 uses for telling the next generation, so the lament ends by taking up the task the previous psalm set.

typology.type: The defiled and ruined temple, Psalm 79:1
typology.fulfillment: The psalm mourns a sanctuary trampled by the nations. Jesus twice acted in the same line of concern, driving out the traders, Matthew 21:12-13, and warning that not one stone would be left on another, Matthew 24:2. He also spoke of 'the temple of His body,' John 2:21, and Paul says the church is now God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16-17, 'a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22. The correspondence is that God still has a holy place that can be violated. The escalation is that the place is now a person and a people, and the type falls short because no stone building, however sacred, can be indestructible.

typology.type: Atonement for the sake of God's name, Psalm 79:9
typology.fulfillment: The psalm asks God to 'atone,' and to do it without any claim of merit. Romans 3:25-26 says God presented Christ as 'the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness,' because He had passed over the sins committed beforehand. The appeal to God's name is met in the cross, where God upholds His own righteousness while justifying the ungodly. Ezekiel 36:22 shows the same logic on God's side: He acts for His holy name. The type falls short because the psalm still asks for a rescue from enemies, while Christ's atonement reaches the deeper enemy, sin itself.

typology.type: The reproach hurled at God, Psalm 79:12
typology.fulfillment: The psalm sees that the neighbors' scorn is directed at God Himself. Paul takes a line from Psalm 69:9, 'The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me,' and applies it to Christ, Romans 15:3. In the passion, the insults that belonged to sinners against God fell on the Son, and Hebrews 13:12-13 calls believers to go outside the camp 'bearing the disgrace He bore.' The correspondence is real: God's people and God's honor are bound together. It escalates because Christ takes the reproach in person. It falls short of a full match because the psalm asks that the reproach be repaid, while Christ bears it and prays for forgiveness.

typology.type: The cry for blood to be avenged, Psalm 79:10
typology.fulfillment: The plea that God make known His vengeance for the bloodshed of His servants is taken up by the martyrs under the altar: 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?' Revelation 6:10. The final answer comes when a great multitude stands before the throne and the Lamb, Revelation 7:9-10, and the heavenly voices sing that His judgments are true and just, Revelation 19:1-2. The type shows that the prayer is heard, but not always at once. It falls short as a pattern for our own conduct, since the cross intervenes: the Lamb who was slain is also the One who will judge.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first through the question it cannot answer alone. The people ask God to atone for sins and to do it for His own name, verses 8-9, yet they have no sacrifice to offer and no temple to offer it in. The way that God can forgive sin without setting aside His own righteousness is the very thing Romans 3:25-26 says the cross demonstrates. God 'passed over the sins committed beforehand,' the same past sins that Asaph asks God not to hold against them, and then showed in Christ how He could do so and still be just and the justifier of those who believe.

It leads to Christ through the reproach. The psalm hears the neighbors' contempt as directed at God, verse 12. Paul takes the same idea, 'The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me,' from Psalm 69:9 and hears it in the mouth of Christ, Romans 15:3. Jesus is the one in whom God's own honor and His people's shame meet, and He bears the disgrace outside the camp, Hebrews 13:12-13.

It leads to Christ through the temple and the city. He is the one who wept over Jerusalem and foretold that its enemies would level it because it did not recognize the time of its visitation, Luke 19:41-44. He stands in the place of the mourner of Psalm 79, grieving over the ruin. Yet He also names Himself the true temple that will be raised, John 2:19-21, so the grief is answered from within the sorrow. Believers are the living stones of the new temple, 1 Peter 2:5 and Ephesians 2:19-22.

It leads to Christ through the wrath. The psalm asks God to pour out His wrath on nations that do not know Him, verse 6. Yet in Gethsemane the Son asked that the cup pass from Him, Matthew 26:39, and then drank it, so that those who were once enemies could be reconciled, Romans 5:9-10. The judgment the psalm calls down on others fell on the Lamb, and the nations that did not call on the name are now invited to call on it.

Finally it leads to Christ through the flock. The people who end the psalm as sheep of God's pasture find their Shepherd in Jesus, who says, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and who holds His sheep so that no one can snatch them out of His hand, John 10:28. Revelation says the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd, Revelation 7:17.

A caution belongs here. The psalm is not a hidden prediction of the cross, and we should not read every detail as a code. The link is that a people who plead nothing but God's name, in a situation that only God can answer, are reaching for what He later gave in Christ.
study.god:
The psalm assumes a God who owns things. The land, the temple, the people and the dead are all His, and the nations who have taken them have struck at Him. Because He owns, He can be petitioned. The whole prayer stands on the belief that what happens to His people happens to Him.

It shows a God who is jealous, verse 5. That is not a small or petty anger. It is the fire of a covenant partner who cannot be indifferent to His people's betrayal or to their suffering. The people understand that His anger against them is a real thing, and they ask how long it will last. They do not deny the anger; they plead against it, as Moses did at Sinai, Exodus 32:11-14. God allows Himself to be argued with.

It shows a God whose name is at stake. 'Why should the nations ask, Where is their God?' verse 10. The name of the LORD is bound to His people in the sight of the world, and He has bound Himself to it. Ezekiel 36:22-23 confirms that God does act for His holy name. That is not vanity, since His glory is the world's good: for a holy God to be seen as weak or absent would be to leave the world without a rescuer.

It shows a God of compassion, rachamim, who is asked to come quickly, verse 8. The people lean on that compassion because they cannot lean on anything else. The mercy of God is presented as the one thing left to appeal to, and it is enough.

It shows a God who is just. The prayers for repayment rest on the belief that violence against His servants will not go unanswered. The verbs of vengeance are addressed to God because He alone judges without malice, as Deuteronomy 32:35-36 says: He will avenge, and He will have compassion on His servants when their strength is gone. The two go together.

It shows a God who hears the groaning of prisoners, verse 11, and has an arm strong enough to preserve those condemned to death. Nothing in the psalm suggests that the situation is under control from a human point of view.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to name what has been lost without hurry, to confess as a body, to hold God to His character in prayer, and to promise thanks before the answer arrives. The last word is not the ruin but a flock that will 'thank You forever.'

crossReferences.note: Micah warned that Jerusalem would become a heap of rubble and the temple mount a wooded ridge. The psalm uses the same word for rubble, so it reads the destruction as the coming true of that warning, and it shows that the disaster was not random but the outcome of a long announced judgment.

The prayer of verses 6 and 7 appears almost word for word in Jeremiah, who prays that God pour out His wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge Him. Two voices of the same crisis ask for the same thing, which suggests that the prayer was shared among those who lived through the fall of Jerusalem.

The covenant curse of unburied corpses, food for the birds and beasts. Psalm 79:2-3 shows this curse in place. The people read their suffering in the light of the law they had broken, and that is why their prayer moves from complaint to confession in verse 8.

A twin lament over the same ruin. It too speaks of God's anger smoldering against the sheep of His pasture and of the enemy burning the sanctuary. Reading the two psalms together shows how the community returned again and again to the same words, and how the grief was worked through in liturgy.

'Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment.' This is one of the ways the 'past sins' of Psalm 79:8 can be read. It shows the exile generation struggling with the weight of inherited guilt while still owning their share of it.

Daniel's prayer in exile has the same shape as verses 8 to 10. He confesses, appeals to God's compassion rather than to righteous acts, and asks for the sake of God's name and city. The sanctuary lies desolate and the appeal is to God's own reputation.

God says He will act, not for Israel's sake, but for His holy name, profaned among the nations. This is the answer, from God's side, to the plea of Psalm 79:9. It shows that the appeal to the name was not a lawyer's trick but an argument God Himself accepts.

Paul forbids revenge and quotes the words, 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.' It supplies the right frame for the psalm's harsh requests: they are given to God, who repays, and are not carried out by the people of God with their own hands.

God passed over former sins in His forbearance and presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate His righteousness. It answers the question behind Psalm 79:8-9, how a holy God can forgive sinners for the sake of His name, and it uses the same language of past sins.

The martyrs under the altar take the cry of Psalm 79:10 into heaven: 'How long, O Lord... until You avenge our blood?' The prayer is not silenced by the cross. It is placed inside the story of the Lamb, with an answer promised and a time set.

Jesus says His sheep listen to His voice, and no one can snatch them from His hand. It is the reply to the flock of Psalm 79:13, exposed to wolves and slaughter, and it shows that the ownership the psalm claimed for God is exercised in Christ.

study.oneStory:
The psalm stands between two acts of the Bible's story. Behind it lies the giving of a land, a city and a temple, the pieces of the inheritance that Exodus 15:17 saw from far off and Psalm 78:54 celebrated as arrived. Ahead of it lies exile, and beyond exile, restoration and something more.

The first question the psalm poses is the one the story keeps asking: what does God do when His people's sin brings the enemy to the gate? Deuteronomy 28 had promised the curse, and 2 Kings 25 reports it. The psalm does not dispute the justice. It brings what is left, the memory of God's name, and asks for mercy. The book of Isaiah answers it with the promise that Jerusalem's iniquity has been pardoned, Isaiah 40:2, and Ezekiel with the promise that God will act for His own name and put a new heart in His people, Ezekiel 36:22-27.

The second question is what will become of the nations. The psalm asks God to pour out wrath on them and to make Himself known among them, verse 10. The rest of the Bible turns the request in a surprising direction. The judgment of the nations is real, but the prophets also see the nations coming to Zion to learn God's ways, and the gospel sends out a people to call on the name that the nations once refused. Paul's word is that God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, and the same Lamb who bears wrath opens the door to every tribe and tongue, Revelation 7:9-10.

The story turns at the cross. There the reproach of God falls on the Son, the atonement the psalm asked for is made, and the vengeance the martyrs still await is held in the hands of the One who died for enemies. Those who were 'sheep to be slaughtered' find a Shepherd who was slaughtered for them.

The story ends in the new creation with no temple, since the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, and with no more groaning of the captive. The Lamb shepherds His people to living water and wipes every tear from their eyes, Revelation 7:17. The vow of Psalm 79:13, to thank Him forever and to tell His praise from generation to generation, becomes the song of the multitude before the throne.

sermon.title: How Much Does God Love This Church?
sermon.why: Piper preaches from Psalm 79, including its appeal to God's name in verse 9, to show how God's own love and glory, not His people's merit, ground His care for a suffering congregation.

quiz.q: What has happened to Jerusalem and the temple according to verses 1-3?

options.text: The nations have invaded, defiled the holy temple, reduced the city to rubble, and left the dead unburied.
options.note: This is the exact devastation described in the opening verses.

options.text: The city has flourished under a period of peace.
options.note: The opposite is true; the psalm opens with ruin and desecration.

options.text: The temple has been rebuilt more gloriously than before.
options.note: The psalm describes destruction, not rebuilding.

options.text: The people have voluntarily abandoned the city.
options.note: The devastation comes from invasion, not voluntary abandonment.

quiz.q: On what basis does the psalmist ask God to help and deliver, in verse 9?

options.text: For the glory of God's own name, not for any merit of the people.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly grounds the plea in God's name and glory.

options.text: Because Israel had kept the law perfectly.
options.note: The psalm openly confesses past sins rather than claiming perfect obedience.

options.text: Because the surrounding nations deserved punishment more than Israel.
options.note: Comparative merit is not the stated basis for the plea.

options.text: Because the people had suffered enough to earn deliverance.
options.note: Suffering is described, but the explicit ground given is God's name, not accumulated merit through suffering.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do regarding the nations, in verse 6?

options.text: Pour out His wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge Him.
options.note: Verse 6 makes this request directly.

options.text: Bless the nations regardless of their actions.
options.note: The request is for God's wrath, not an unconditional blessing.

options.text: Ignore the nations entirely and focus only on Israel.
options.note: The nations are directly addressed, not ignored.

options.text: Make peace with the nations without addressing their sin.
options.note: The plea calls for justice on the nations' unacknowledged wrongdoing, not simple peace.

quiz.q: What vow does the psalm make once God acts, in verse 13?

options.text: God's people, the sheep of His pasture, will thank Him forever, from generation to generation.
options.note: This is the closing vow of the psalm.

options.text: The people will never trust God again after such suffering.
options.note: The psalm ends in a vow of praise, not lasting distrust.

options.text: The people will seek out other gods for greater protection.
options.note: The psalm's confidence remains fixed on the LORD alone.

options.text: The people will praise God only until the next crisis arises.
options.note: The vow is for perpetual, generational praise, not a temporary response.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's plea for atonement point toward the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates the atonement God provides in Christ, for His own name's sake rather than human merit.
options.note: Romans 3:25-26 shows God Himself providing atonement through Christ on this same basis.

options.text: It has no connection to New Testament teaching on atonement.
options.note: The plea for atonement grounded in God's name directly anticipates the gospel's logic.

options.text: It teaches that atonement must always be earned through suffering.
options.note: The psalm explicitly asks for atonement as a gift for God's name's sake, not as something earned.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of the temple's rebuilding.
options.note: The psalm addresses atonement and deliverance, not a specific rebuilding timeline.

questions: The psalmist names the devastation honestly before God rather than minimizing it, verses 1-4. What pain or loss are you tempted to minimize instead of bringing honestly to God in prayer?
The plea in verse 9 rests entirely on God's own name and glory, not on Israel's merit. Where are you trying to earn God's help instead of resting on His character and promises in Christ?
The psalm asks God to redirect His righteous anger toward those who reject Him, verses 5-7. How do you hold together honest anger at injustice with trust in God's own timing and justice?

Even after admitting 'past sins,' the psalmist asks for God's compassion to 'come quickly,' verse 8. What sin do you need to confess honestly today, trusting that God's compassion, not your track record, is your hope?
The psalm ends with a vow to praise God forever once He acts, verse 13. What would it look like for you to vow praise now, even before your circumstances change?

translationNotes.note: 'Inheritance' (nachalah) frames the ruin of Jerusalem and the temple not merely as a national tragedy but as an affront to what belongs to God Himself.
'Atone' (kipper) asks God to provide the covering for sin Himself, on the ground of His own name and glory rather than the people's merit.
'The sheep of Your pasture' (tson) closes the psalm with covenant shepherd imagery that recurs across this cluster of psalms and finds its fulfillment in Christ the Good Shepherd.
